q: This painter killed a man in a brawl in Rome and fled to Malta. He used dramatic contrasts of light and dark called tenebrism, as in his Judith Beheading Holofernes. His Calling of Saint Matthew hangs in the Contarelli Chapel in San Luigi dei Francesi. For 10 points, name this Italian Baroque master.

This Spanish court painter made a portrait of Pope Innocent X and the Rokeby Venus. His masterpiece shows the Infanta Margarita surrounded by attendants, with the artist himself standing at an easel. For 10 points, name this painter of Las Meninas who served Philip IV.

This French painter caused scandals with a nude woman gazing at the viewer in Olympia and with a picnic scene showing a naked woman beside clothed men. His last major work shows a barmaid at the Folies-Bergère. For 10 points, name this artist of Luncheon on the Grass.

This Post-Impressionist from Aix-en-Provence painted many views of Mont Sainte-Victoire. He also painted The Card Players and several groups of bathers. His method of building form from planes of color influenced the Cubists. For 10 points, name this painter.

This Frenchman worked briefly with Van Gogh in Arles, then left for Tahiti. His paintings include Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going? and use flat areas of bold color. For 10 points, name this Post-Impressionist who painted Tahitian women.

This Austrian artist was a founder of the Vienna Secession and used gold leaf in his portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer. His painting of a couple embracing, with patterned robes, is called The Kiss. For 10 points, name this Symbolist painter.

This Italian painted the fresco The School of Athens in the Vatican's Stanza della Segnatura. He also made the Sistine Madonna and worked in Rome under Pope Julius II. He died in 1520 at age thirty-seven. For 10 points, name this Renaissance painter.

This Flemish painter used oil glazes to produce intensely detailed pictures. His Ghent Altarpiece was made with his brother Hubert. A convex mirror in the background of his Arnolfini Portrait reflects the room. For 10 points, name this Early Netherlandish painter.

This Flemish Baroque painter ran a huge workshop in Antwerp and painted full-figured nudes and swirling allegories. He made the cycle of the life of Marie de' Medici and The Descent from the Cross. For 10 points, name this artist.

This Spanish painter made a harrowing image of an execution by French soldiers, The Third of May 1808. His late Black Paintings include Saturn Devouring His Son. His series The Disasters of War depicts atrocities. For 10 points, name this artist of The Naked Maja.

This French Romantic painter showed a bare-breasted woman waving the tricolor flag over a barricade in Liberty Leading the People. His Death of Sardanapalus is filled with color and violence. For 10 points, name this rival of Ingres.

This French painter depicted the murdered revolutionary Jean-Paul Marat in his bath. His Oath of the Horatii is a prime example of Neoclassicism, and he later served as Napoleon's court painter. For 10 points, name this artist of The Death of Marat.

This movement was announced in a 1924 manifesto by André Breton. Its artists such as Max Ernst and René Magritte tried to express the unconscious through dreamlike images and automatic drawing. For 10 points, name this movement associated with Dalí.

This Belgian painter's The Treachery of Images shows a pipe with a caption saying it is not a pipe. He also painted a man in a bowler hat with an apple obscuring his face in The Son of Man. For 10 points, name this Surrealist.

This Norwegian painter made multiple versions of a figure on a bridge clutching its face as the sky turns blood red. He also painted Madonna and The Sick Child. His works helped found Expressionism. For 10 points, name this artist of The Scream.

This Catalan artist painted Harlequin's Carnival and made a series of works called Constellations. His biomorphic Surrealist paintings feature stars, eyes, and playful black lines on bright backgrounds. For 10 points, name this Spanish artist of The Farm.

This Latvian-born American painter produced large canvases with floating blocks of color for the Seagram Building and a chapel in Houston. He is a leading figure of Color Field painting. For 10 points, name this artist of the Rothko Chapel.

This artist enlarged panels from comic books, using Ben-Day dots and bold outlines. His works include Drowning Girl and Whaam!, which depicts a fighter plane firing at another. For 10 points, name this American pop artist.

This African-American painter made sixty panels about the Great Migration in a series with short captions. He also painted scenes of Harlem and studied at the Harlem Art Workshop. For 10 points, name this artist of The Migration Series.

This American painter's portrait of Virginie Gautreau, titled Madame X, caused a scandal at the 1884 Paris Salon. He painted high-society portraits in London and Boston. For 10 points, name this artist of Carnation, Lily, Lily, Rose.

This Italian sculptor carved The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa and designed the baldachin and colonnade at Saint Peter's. His marble Apollo and Daphne appears to capture a mid-transformation. For 10 points, name this master of Baroque sculpture.

This English Romantic painter showed a warship being towed to its last berth in The Fighting Temeraire. His Rain, Steam and Speed depicts a train on a bridge. His later paintings dissolve forms in light. For 10 points, name this artist.

This group formed in 1848 and rejected the formulas taught by the Royal Academy. Its members included John Everett Millais, who painted Ophelia, and Dante Gabriel Rossetti. They wanted to return to the clarity of art before the Italian Renaissance. For 10 points, name this British brotherhood.

This Dutch painter made The Garden of Earthly Delights, a triptych with a paradise panel, a middle panel full of nudes, and a panel of hell with monstrous creatures. His other works include The Haywain. For 10 points, name this artist.

This Flemish painter portrayed peasants in works such as Hunters in the Snow and The Peasant Wedding. He also painted The Tower of Babel. His sons were also painters. For 10 points, name this artist, sometimes called "the Elder."

This early twentieth-century movement is named after a critic's description of its artists as "wild beasts." Henri Matisse and André Derain used pure, unnatural colors in works such as Woman with a Hat. For 10 points, name this movement.

This eighteenth-century French style favored pastel colors, curves, and playful scenes. Fragonard's The Swing and Boucher's paintings of Madame de Pompadour are examples. It followed the Baroque. For 10 points, name this lighthearted style.

This Florentine painted frescoes in the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua. His figures show weight and emotion, breaking with the flatter Byzantine style. He also designed the campanile of Florence's cathedral. For 10 points, name this painter often called a forerunner of the Renaissance.

This anti-art movement began at Zurich's Cabaret Voltaire in 1916 in reaction to World War I. Its works mocked bourgeois values and used nonsense, collage, and chance. Hugo Ball and Hans Arp were participants. For 10 points, name this movement.

This French artist scandalized the 1913 Armory Show with Nude Descending a Staircase, No. 2. He submitted a signed porcelain urinal as Fountain and coined the term "readymade." For 10 points, name this Dada artist.

q: This Hungarian pianist wrote the Hungarian Rhapsodies and invented the symphonic poem. He was a famed virtuoso who caused near-hysteria among fans, a phenomenon called "Lisztomania." For 10 points, name this composer of Les préludes.

This composer was a child prodigy who wrote an overture to A Midsummer Night's Dream at age seventeen. He revived interest in Bach's Saint Matthew Passion. His sister Fanny was also a composer. For 10 points, name this German composer of the Wedding March.

This Italian composer wrote the operas Rigoletto, La traviata, and Aida. His Requiem is considered a dramatic work, and "La donna è mobile" is from one of his operas. For 10 points, name this composer of Otello and Falstaff.

This Czech composer spent three years in the United States and wrote his Symphony No. 9 "From the New World." He also wrote the Slavonic Dances and the opera Rusalka. For 10 points, name this composer.

This Austrian composer wrote symphonies of huge scale, including the Resurrection and the Symphony of a Thousand. He also wrote Das Lied von der Erde and Kindertotenlieder. For 10 points, name this Bohemian-born conductor and composer.

This Norwegian composer wrote incidental music for Ibsen's play Peer Gynt, including "In the Hall of the Mountain King." He also wrote a famous piano concerto in A minor. For 10 points, name this composer.
This Finnish composer wrote the tone poem Finlandia, which became a symbol of national identity. He also wrote seven symphonies and The Swan of Tuonela. For 10 points, name this composer.

This Russian pianist and composer wrote four piano concertos, including the Second, and the Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini. After leaving Russia in 1917 he settled in the United States. For 10 points, name this Romantic composer.

This Soviet composer wrote fifteen symphonies, including the Leningrad Symphony. He had a complicated relationship with Stalin's government and wrote the opera Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District. For 10 points, name this composer.

This French composer wrote a work that begins with a snare drum rhythm and slowly builds with a single repeated melody. He also wrote Pavane for a Dead Princess and orchestrated Pictures at an Exhibition. For 10 points, name this composer of Boléro.

This Hungarian composer collected folk songs with Zoltán Kodály. He wrote Concerto for Orchestra and the opera Bluebeard's Castle. His six string quartets are central works of the twentieth century. For 10 points, name this composer of Mikrokosmos.

This Italian composer wrote The Barber of Seville and an overture to an opera about a Swiss archer, William Tell. The final part of that overture is used as a theme for The Lone Ranger. For 10 points, name this composer.

This French composer wrote an opera set in Seville about a gypsy factory worker, which includes the "Habanera" and the "Toreador Song." He also wrote the L'Arlésienne suites. For 10 points, name this composer of Carmen.

This French composer wrote a suite for chamber orchestra that includes movements on the elephant, the swan, and fossils. His Symphony No. 3 has a part for organ. For 10 points, name this composer of Danse macabre and Carnival of the Animals.

This Russian composer wrote a piano suite inspired by an exhibition of paintings by his friend Viktor Hartmann. He also wrote the opera Boris Godunov and the tone poem Night on Bald Mountain. For 10 points, name this member of The Five.

This French composer wrote Symphonie fantastique, a work with an idée fixe representing the artist's beloved. He also wrote the opera Les Troyens and a treatise on orchestration. For 10 points, name this Romantic composer.
This African-American composer's "Maple Leaf Rag" became a hit in 1899. He also wrote "The Entertainer," which was used in the film The Sting. For 10 points, name this "King of Ragtime."

This trumpeter led a quintet that made Kind of Blue in 1959, with John Coltrane on saxophone. He pioneered cool jazz and later electric jazz fusion with Bitches Brew. For 10 points, name this jazz musician.

This American singer was nicknamed the "First Lady of Song." She was known for her scat singing and for songbook albums of Cole Porter and George Gershwin. For 10 points, name this jazz vocalist who recorded "Summertime" with Louis Armstrong.

This singer-songwriter wrote "Blowin' in the Wind" and "The Times They Are a-Changin'." He went electric at the 1965 Newport Folk Festival and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2016. For 10 points, name this artist of Highway 61 Revisited.

This type of piece features a soloist playing against an orchestra, usually with three movements: fast, slow, fast. Examples include Beethoven's Emperor and Tchaikovsky's one for violin. For 10 points, name this kind of work.

This woodwind instrument has a single reed and a cylindrical bore. Benny Goodman was a famous jazz player of it, and Mozart wrote a famous concerto for it. For 10 points, name this instrument whose lower register is called the chalumeau.

This string instrument is held between the knees and played with a bow. Yo-Yo Ma plays it, and Bach wrote six unaccompanied suites for it. It is tuned a fifth lower than a viola. For 10 points, name this instrument.
This form of unaccompanied, monophonic sacred song was codified in the Middle Ages and named for a pope. It is sung in Latin without harmony by monks. For 10 points, name this type of chant.

In a concerto, this is an unaccompanied passage for the soloist, often improvised in the classical era. It usually comes near the end of a movement, before the orchestra returns. For 10 points, name this showy passage.

This English Baroque composer wrote the opera Dido and Aeneas, which includes "When I am laid in earth." He worked in the Chapel Royal and wrote Come Ye Sons of Art. For 10 points, name this composer.

This Italian composer's L'Orfeo from 1607 is one of the earliest operas still regularly performed. He wrote the Vespers of 1610 and worked at Saint Mark's in Venice. For 10 points, name this composer.

This Viennese composer was called the "Waltz King." He wrote the Blue Danube and the operetta Die Fledermaus. His father, who wrote the Radetzky March, shared his name. For 10 points, name this composer.

This American composer and conductor wrote the music for West Side Story and led the New York Philharmonic. He also wrote Candide and the Chichester Psalms. For 10 points, name this man who gave televised Young People's Concerts.

q: This peak in the Sierra Nevada is the highest in the contiguous United States, at over fourteen thousand feet. It lies on the border of Inyo and Tulare counties in California. The town of Lone Pine sits at its eastern base. For 10 points, name this mountain.

This deep alpine lake on the California-Nevada border is known for its clear blue water. It lies in a basin of the Sierra Nevada and has ski resorts such as Heavenly nearby. Emerald Bay is on its southwestern shore. For 10 points, name this lake.

This Kentucky national park protects the longest known cave system in the world. Its passages have been explored for more than four hundred miles. Visitors tour its chambers such as the Rotunda. For 10 points, name this cave.

This New Mexico national park in the Guadalupe Mountains has a huge chamber called the Big Room. Millions of bats emerge from its entrance at dusk. It is named for a nearby city. For 10 points, name these limestone caves.

Clingmans Dome is the highest point in this mountain range on the Tennessee-North Carolina border. The Cades Cove valley lies within it. Blue mist often hangs over its slopes. For 10 points, name this part of the Appalachians whose national park takes its name.

John Muir called this range the "Range of Light." It stretches along the eastern edge of California and includes Yosemite and Sequoia national parks. Its eastern face rises steeply above the Owens Valley. For 10 points, name this mountain range.

This volcanic mountain range runs from northern California through Oregon and Washington. It includes Mount Rainier, Mount Hood, and Mount Shasta. It is part of the Pacific Ring of Fire. For 10 points, name this range of the Pacific Northwest.

This river of the northwestern United States flows through Idaho's Hells Canyon and past Lewiston. It begins in Wyoming near Jackson Hole and joins the Columbia River in Washington. Shoshone Falls is on it. For 10 points, name this river.

This river flows south from the Adirondacks past Albany to New York Harbor. The Palisades and West Point lie along it. It is named for an English explorer who sailed on it in 1609. For 10 points, name this river.

This waterway opened in 1825 and connected Albany to Buffalo. It was nicknamed "Clinton's Ditch" for the governor who championed it. It made New York City the nation's leading port. For 10 points, name this man-made channel linking the Hudson River to Lake Erie.

Brooklyn and Queens are on this island, which stretches east from New York City. It includes the Hamptons and Montauk Point on its eastern end. Fire Island lies off its south shore. For 10 points, name this large island of New York State.

This chain of barrier islands off North Carolina includes Kitty Hawk and Roanoke Island. The lost colony of Roanoke was here, and the Wright brothers flew nearby. Hurricanes frequently erode its narrow sands. For 10 points, name these islands on the Atlantic coast.

This range in South Dakota and Wyoming is sacred to the Lakota. Gold was discovered there in 1874, leading to the town of Deadwood. Crazy Horse Memorial is carved into one of its mountains. For 10 points, name these hills.

Eroded buttes and pinnacles with colorful strata mark this national park in South Dakota. Its name was given by the Lakota. Bighorn sheep and prairie dogs live on its grasslands. For 10 points, name this dry landscape.

This highland region in Missouri, Arkansas, and Oklahoma is a forested plateau, not a true mountain range. Branson and a large reservoir on the Osage River are in it. Its caves and springs are typical of karst terrain. For 10 points, name this region of the central United States.

This large shallow lake in south-central Florida drains into the Everglades. A dike built after hurricanes in the 1920s surrounds it. Its name comes from a Seminole word for "big water." For 10 points, name this lake.

This river rises in the San Juan Mountains of Colorado and flows through Albuquerque and El Paso. It forms part of the border between Texas and Mexico. It reaches the Gulf of Mexico near Brownsville. For 10 points, name this river.

Sandstone buttes such as the Mittens rise from the desert floor in this Navajo Tribal Park on the Utah-Arizona border. Many Western films by John Ford were shot there. For 10 points, name this red-rock landscape.

This Wyoming rock formation, a column of igneous rock, was declared the first national monument in 1906. Its sides are fluted columns. It was featured in the film Close Encounters of the Third Kind. For 10 points, name this tower.

This Oregon lake fills the caldera of Mount Mazama, which erupted about 7,700 years ago. Wizard Island rises from it. It is the deepest lake in the United States. For 10 points, name this national park lake.

El Capitan and Half Dome rise above this California valley. Ansel Adams photographed its waterfalls, and John Muir campaigned to protect it. Glaciers carved its granite walls. For 10 points, name this national park in the Sierra Nevada.

This chain of volcanic islands stretches west from the Alaska Peninsula toward Russia. Dutch Harbor is a major fishing port there. Japan invaded Attu and Kiska in World War II. For 10 points, name this archipelago.

This fault runs through California for hundreds of miles, where the Pacific Plate slides past the North American Plate. Slippage on it caused the 1906 earthquake in San Francisco. For 10 points, name this transform fault.

This large region of the western United States has no outlet to the sea, so its rivers drain into salt flats and lakes. It includes most of Nevada and part of Utah. Bristlecone pines grow in its mountains. For 10 points, name this high desert.

This desert covers much of southern Arizona and northwestern Mexico. The tall saguaro cactus grows there, and it has two rainy seasons each year. Phoenix and Tucson are in it. For 10 points, name this desert.

This line in the Rocky Mountains separates rivers that flow toward the Atlantic and Gulf from those that flow toward the Pacific. It follows peaks from New Mexico to Montana. For 10 points, name this feature, whose Triple Divide Peak is in Glacier National Park.

This point is the only place in the United States where four states meet. They are Utah, Colorado, New Mexico, and Arizona. A monument marks the spot on Navajo land. For 10 points, name this location.
Seneca and Cayuga are among these long narrow lakes in central New York, carved by glaciers. Ithaca sits at the south end of one. The region is known for wineries. For 10 points, name these lakes.

This capital of Colorado is called the Mile High City because its elevation is about 5,280 feet. It lies where the Great Plains meet the Rocky Mountains. Coors Field is there. For 10 points, name this city.

The Space Needle, built for the 1962 World's Fair, rises over this city in Washington State. It lies between Puget Sound and Lake Washington. Pike Place Market is there. For 10 points, name this city.

This lake north of New Orleans is crossed by a very long causeway. It is brackish and connects to the Gulf of Mexico through passes. Its name honors a French minister. For 10 points, name this Louisiana lake.

q: This river rises in the Black Forest of Germany and flows past Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest, and Belgrade. Its delta in Romania is a wildlife reserve. It empties into the Black Sea. For 10 points, name this second-longest river in Europe.

This river begins in the Swiss Alps and flows north past Basel, Cologne, and Rotterdam to the North Sea. Its Middle Rhine gorge is famous for castles and the Lorelei rock. Barges carry heavy cargo along it. For 10 points, name this European river.

This longest river in Europe flows through Russia past Kazan, Nizhny Novgorod, and Volgograd. It ends in a large delta on the Caspian Sea. It is called "Mother" in Russian folk tradition. For 10 points, name this river.

This river is sacred to Hindus and flows past Varanasi. Its tributary, the Yamuna, joins it at Allahabad. Its delta, shared with Bangladesh, empties into the Bay of Bengal. For 10 points, name this river of northern India.

This river in central Africa crosses the equator twice. The capitals Kinshasa and Brazzaville face each other across it. It is the deepest river in the world. For 10 points, name this river, which empties into the Atlantic Ocean.

This waterfall on the Zambezi River lies on the border of Zambia and Zimbabwe. David Livingstone named it for a British queen. Its local name means "the smoke that thunders." For 10 points, name this falls.
This is the largest lake in Africa, shared by Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania. John Hanning Speke named it in 1858. It is the main source of the White Nile. For 10 points, name this lake.

This lake in southern Siberia is the deepest lake in the world and holds a large share of the planet's unfrozen fresh water. Irkutsk is nearby. The nerpa seal lives only here. For 10 points, name this lake.

The cities of Baku and Astrakhan lie on this largest inland body of water, which has no outlet to the ocean. Kazakhstan, Iran, Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan, and Russia surround it. It is famous for its sturgeon, source of caviar. For 10 points, name this body of water.

Odessa and Varna are ports on this sea, which connects to the Mediterranean via the Bosphorus. The Danube empties into it. Constanta in Romania and Batumi in Georgia are ports on it. For 10 points, name this sea between Europe and Asia.

The shore of this salt lake, between Israel and Jordan, is the lowest land elevation on Earth. Swimmers float easily on it because it is so salty. Scrolls were found in caves at Qumran near it. For 10 points, name this sea fed by the Jordan River.

This sea separates Africa from the Arabian Peninsula. Its northern end splits into the Gulf of Suez and the Gulf of Aqaba. Eritrea and Saudi Arabia lie on its coasts. For 10 points, name this sea that Moses parts in the Book of Exodus.
The Strait of Hormuz links this body of water to the Gulf of Oman. Kuwait, Bahrain, and Qatar lie on it. Iran lies on its northern coast. For 10 points, name this gulf, rich in oil.

Knossos, the palace of the Minoan civilization, is on this largest Greek island. Its capital and largest city is Heraklion. In myth, King Minos kept the Minotaur in a labyrinth here, and Zeus was said to have been raised in one of its caves. For 10 points, name this island south of the Aegean Sea.

This desert in northern Chile is considered the driest non-polar desert on Earth. Parts of it have gone without rain for years. Its nitrate deposits once caused wars. For 10 points, name this desert west of the Andes.

This semi-arid sandy region covers much of Botswana and parts of Namibia and South Africa. The San people have lived there for thousands of years. The Okavango Delta lies in it. For 10 points, name this southern African desert.

Each year, huge herds of wildebeest and zebras migrate across this ecosystem in northern Tanzania. Its name comes from a Maasai word meaning "endless plains." Ngorongoro Crater lies nearby. For 10 points, name this national park and plain.
This island nation in the North Atlantic sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Its capital is Reykjavik. It is known for geysers, glaciers like Vatnajokull, and volcanoes. For 10 points, name this country.

Palermo and Catania are cities on this largest island in the Mediterranean Sea. Mount Etna is a volcano on it. The Strait of Messina separates it from the Italian mainland. For 10 points, name this island south of Italy.
This high plateau north of the Himalayas is sometimes called the "Roof of the World." Lhasa lies on it. Many major Asian rivers begin there. For 10 points, name this plateau, located mostly in China.

These mountains run north to south through Russia and are the traditional boundary between Europe and Asia. Yekaterinburg lies at their eastern foot. Rich mineral deposits have been mined there. For 10 points, name this range.
This range separates the Iberian Peninsula from the rest of Europe. The tiny country of Andorra lies within it. Its high point is Aneto. For 10 points, name these mountains between Spain and France.

Olduvai Gorge and Lake Tanganyika lie within this long fault system in East Africa, where tectonic plates are pulling apart. It extends from the Red Sea region south to Mozambique. Many early hominid fossils have been found along it. For 10 points, name this trough.

Challenger Deep, the deepest known point in the oceans, lies in this feature of the western Pacific. It lies near the island of Guam. The Trieste carried two men to its bottom in 1960. For 10 points, name this deep trench.

This lake on the border of Peru and Bolivia is one of the highest large navigable lakes in the world. The Uros people live on floating islands made of reeds. It lies on the Altiplano in the Andes. For 10 points, name this lake.

This waterfall in Venezuela is the tallest in the world. It plunges from the flat summit of Auyan-tepui. Its English name honors a pilot who landed his plane on the plateau above it. For 10 points, name this falls.

The Drake Passage lies just south of this headland, the southernmost tip of South America's Tierra del Fuego archipelago. Sailors have long feared its storms and high waves. It belongs to Chile. For 10 points, name this cape.
Bartolomeu Dias rounded this cape in 1488 and called it the Cape of Storms. It is near Cape Town, South Africa. Its later name inspired hope of a sea route to India. For 10 points, name this cape.

This narrow strait connects the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara. It passes through Istanbul and is crossed by several suspension bridges. It forms part of the boundary between Europe and Asia. For 10 points, name this strait.

This region at the southern end of South America is divided between Argentina and Chile. Perito Moreno Glacier is in it. Its steppe is home to guanacos and penguins. For 10 points, name this windswept region.

The cone of this volcano in Japan is nearly symmetrical and rises to about 3,776 meters. It last erupted in 1707. Climbers ascend it in summer, and snow covers its peak. For 10 points, name this sacred mountain west of Tokyo.

q: This Serbian-American engineer developed the alternating-current induction motor and the coil that bears his name. He worked briefly for Thomas Edison before partnering with George Westinghouse. The unit of magnetic flux density is named for him. For 10 points, name this inventor.

This Scottish scientist noticed in 1928 that a mold had killed bacteria in a dish at Saint Mary's Hospital in London. The mold was Penicillium. He shared the 1945 Nobel Prize for the discovery of the first true antibiotic. For 10 points, name this man who discovered penicillin.

This French chemist developed a vaccine for rabies in 1885 and treated a boy named Joseph Meister. He disproved spontaneous generation and championed germ theory. A process that heats liquids to kill microbes is named for him. For 10 points, name this scientist.

This German physicist discovered X-rays in 1895 in Wurzburg. He made an image of his wife's hand showing her bones. In 1901 he received the first Nobel Prize in Physics. For 10 points, name this scientist.

This Swedish chemist and engineer invented dynamite in 1867. His will left money for prizes in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, and peace. He owned an armaments company. For 10 points, name this man for whom a set of annual prizes is named.

This American inventor patented the cotton gin in 1793, which sped the separation of seeds from cotton fibers. He later promoted interchangeable parts in making muskets. He graduated from Yale. For 10 points, name this man.

This automaker introduced the Model T in 1908 and started a moving assembly line at Highland Park in 1913. He offered workers a five-dollar day. His company was based in Dearborn, Michigan. For 10 points, name this American industrialist.

This Austrian friar studied traits in pea plants in the garden of his monastery in Brno. His 1866 paper described dominant and recessive factors. His work was largely ignored until about 1900. For 10 points, name this founder of genetics.

This British mathematician helped break the Enigma cipher at Bletchley Park during World War II. He proposed an abstract computing machine in 1936. A test for machine intelligence is named for him. For 10 points, name this man.

This woman, a daughter of Lord Byron, wrote notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, including what is considered the first computer program. She was an English mathematician. A programming language is named for her. For 10 points, name this Countess of Lovelace.

This British scientist at CERN proposed a system of linked hypertext documents in 1989. He wrote the first web browser and server. He created HTML and HTTP. For 10 points, name this inventor of the World Wide Web.

Michelangelo painted the ceiling of this chapel in the Vatican between 1508 and 1512. Its fresco The Creation of Adam shows two fingers nearly touching. New popes are chosen in conclave inside it. For 10 points, name this papal chapel.

This Roman temple is topped by a concrete dome with a round opening called the oculus. The emperor Hadrian rebuilt it around 126 CE. The artist Raphael is buried there. For 10 points, name this well-preserved temple in Rome.

The Treasury, or Al-Khazneh, is carved into the rose-colored sandstone cliffs of this ancient city in Jordan. The Nabataeans built it, and visitors enter through a narrow canyon called the Siq. It appeared in an Indiana Jones film. For 10 points, name this archaeological site.

Suryavarman II built this temple in Cambodia in the twelfth century. It features five towers that resemble lotus buds and miles of carved reliefs. It was originally Hindu and later became Buddhist. For 10 points, name this temple complex near Siem Reap.
Jorn Utzon designed this performing arts center whose roof resembles sails. It stands on Bennelong Point in Sydney Harbour and opened in 1973. For 10 points, name this building in Australia.

Construction began on this tower in 1173, and the soil under one side soon began to sink. Galileo is said to have dropped balls from it. It is a freestanding bell tower of a cathedral in Tuscany. For 10 points, name this tilted tower.
This Roman city was buried by ash when Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE. Excavations found plaster casts of victims. Its nearby sister town was Herculaneum. For 10 points, name this city near Naples.

El Castillo, a step pyramid dedicated to the feathered serpent Kukulcan, stands at this Maya site in the Yucatan. The pyramid casts a serpent-shaped shadow at the equinoxes. A large ball court is also here. For 10 points, name this archaeological site.

This hilltop palace and fortress in Granada, Spain, was built by the Nasrid rulers. Its Court of the Lions has a fountain supported by twelve stone lions. It is a masterpiece of Moorish architecture. For 10 points, name this complex.

This set of annual awards was created through the will of a Hungarian-American newspaper publisher. Columbia University administers it. Categories include journalism, fiction, poetry, and music. For 10 points, name this prize first awarded in 1917.
The Soviet Union launched this first artificial satellite on October 4, 1957. It beeped as it circled the Earth. Its launch began the space race. For 10 points, name this satellite.

This telescope was launched aboard Space Shuttle Discovery in 1990. Its main mirror had a flaw that was fixed during a 1993 repair mission. It is named for an astronomer who showed that the universe contains many galaxies. For 10 points, name this orbiting observatory.

This ancient network of trade routes connected China with the Mediterranean. Silk, spices, and ideas traveled along it. Cities such as Samarkand and Kashgar grew rich from it. For 10 points, name this system.

Antonio Stradivari of Cremona, Italy, made string instruments prized for their sound. Some of his violins sell for millions of dollars. They were made in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. For 10 points, name this family of famous violins.

Between 1892 and 1954, millions of immigrants were processed at this small island in New York Harbor. It is now a museum. Statue of Liberty is a short ferry ride away. For 10 points, name this island.

This Albanian-born nun founded the Missionaries of Charity in Calcutta. She worked among the poor and dying and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979. The Catholic Church canonized her in 2016. For 10 points, name this woman.

This Jewish teenager hid with her family in a secret annex in Amsterdam during World War II. Her diary was published after her death at Bergen-Belsen. Her father Otto survived. For 10 points, name this author of The Diary of a Young Girl.
This British primatologist began studying chimpanzees at Gombe Stream in Tanzania in 1960. She observed them using tools. She worked with Louis Leakey. For 10 points, name this scientist.

This French explorer co-invented the Aqualung with Emile Gagnan and sailed the research ship Calypso. He made documentaries including The Silent World. His work promoted ocean conservation. For 10 points, name this undersea explorer.

q: This council was convened by the emperor Constantine in 325 and met in a city in what is now Turkey. It condemned the teachings of the priest Arius, who denied that Christ was fully divine. Its delegates used the term homoousios, meaning of the same substance, to describe the Son and the Father. For 10 points, name this first ecumenical council of the Church, which produced an early creed.

This North African bishop wrote a spiritual autobiography after a conversion in a garden in Milan, where he heard a child's voice say take up and read. His mother Monica prayed for him, and he had earlier followed the Manichaeans. He also wrote The City of God after the sack of Rome in 410. For 10 points, name this bishop of Hippo, author of the Confessions.

After seeing a vision of a cross in the sky before the Battle of the Milvian Bridge in 312, this Roman emperor attributed his victory to the Christian God. He issued the Edict of Milan, which granted religious tolerance, and later founded a new capital on the Bosporus. For 10 points, name this emperor, who is said to have been baptized shortly before his death.

In 1054, representatives of the pope and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated each other in this event. Disputes over papal authority and over the addition of the filioque to the Nicene Creed helped cause it. For 10 points, name this split that divided the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches.

This French reformer wrote the Institutes of the Christian Religion at age twenty-six. He made Geneva a model Protestant city and taught that God has chosen those who will be saved. His followers became the Reformed churches, including the Presbyterians. For 10 points, name this theologian whose ideas are called Calvinism.

This king asked the pope to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon because she had not borne a surviving son. When the pope refused, he had Parliament pass the Act of Supremacy, naming himself the head of the Church of England. For 10 points, name this Tudor king, who married six times.

This Catholic gathering met in an Italian city from 1545 to 1563 under Pope Paul III and his successors. It reaffirmed the seven sacraments, upheld the authority of tradition alongside scripture, and set up seminaries to train priests. It was the main response of the Catholic Church to the Protestant Reformation. For 10 points, name this council of the Counter-Reformation.

This English clergyman and his brother Charles formed a Holy Club at Oxford, whose members were mocked as Methodists for their disciplined habits. After a heartwarming experience at Aldersgate in 1738, he began preaching outdoors to miners and workers. For 10 points, name this founder of Methodism.

This German monk taught at the University of Wittenberg and was summoned to the Diet of Worms in 1521. Hidden afterward at Wartburg Castle, he translated the New Testament into German. For 10 points, name this man who started the Protestant Reformation.

This scholar of the fourth century lived in a cave in Bethlehem while translating the Bible into Latin at the request of Pope Damasus. His version became the standard Bible of the Western Church for over a thousand years. For 10 points, name this saint, the patron of translators and author of the Vulgate.

Printed around 1455 in Mainz, this was the first major book produced in Europe with movable metal type. About 180 copies were made, some on vellum. For 10 points, name this edition of the Latin Bible, named for its printer.

In this Old Testament book, a righteous man loses his children, wealth, and health after Satan challenges his faith with God's permission. His three friends insist that he must have sinned. At last God answers him from a whirlwind. For 10 points, name this book, whose title character is known for his patience.

The apostle Paul wrote this longest of his letters to the Christian community in the capital of the empire. It argues that people are justified by faith rather than by works of the law. Augustine and Martin Luther both drew on it. For 10 points, name this New Testament epistle.
